title: Gen. Casey Answers Questions from Local Media about Ft. Leonard Wood Tornado Damage
description: B-roll of how the USO building has been transformed to warehouse clothes, food, toys and furniture for victims of the New Years Eve EF3 Tornado that destroyed 30 military houses on the installation.  Gen. George Casey, Army Chief of Staff tours the relief donations, visits with volunteers and answers questions from the local media.  Also available in High Definition.
unit_name: Fort Leonard Wood Public Affairs Office

transcript.text: to 35th and we volunteer today helping us gather that's our intake room which used to be our recreation game room is now our intake room
Our volunteers have done such a great job of organizing
I would actually go over here and always come and look at this.
Make a couple comments here and I'd be happy to take questions from you.
I'm General George Casey, I'm the Army Chief of Staff and I came down here to get my first hand looked at
the damage of the tornado because I was thinking about this and I've been in the Army over 40 years and I don't remember an Army installation
getting hit by a natural disaster of this magnitude. I don't remember so many families being displaced so I had to come out and kind of see things for myself.
As I went around today and kind of went to throw the path of the tornado that the things that I really saw were resilience and teamwork
and I was just amazed at the resilience of our soldiers and our families and amazed at the teamwork not only on the installation but between the installation and the local community.
And the progress that's already been made in just a short period of time is a great example of that teamwork and the goods and things that you see behind me here
that have been assembled by the USO and the installation from people on post and from people off post to help the families that have been impacted by this.
It's just an amazing outpouring of support.
And so I want to thank all of the people in the local community for the support that they have given our soldiers and families
not just today but what they do every day to make their lives easier.
And with that I'd be happy to take some questions.
What sort of thing, if this was a deadly photo outside of the post, what sort of things differently maybe just like army people do that other people don't do that keeps them safe?
It's interesting you say that.
You know I've lived on Army Post listen to the warnings and things that come out on television and when I talk to the first couple today,
actually I talked to several couples that had emergency radios, inter-bedrooms, that broadcast an alarm.
And so they had about 15 minutes warning and then one of them had plans and they already knew where they were going to go
and what they were going to do and I wouldn't say they'd practice it but they had thought through it in their own minds.
And you know I talked to a family that had went to a closet, got in the closet, husband, wife, child, dog and that was about the only thing,
that closet was about the only thing in that house left standing.
In fact that they were so, things were so compacted against the closet they actually had to pass their child out and do a whole
and then they finally got themselves out a little bit later.
So I think it's they were very disciplined in their reaction and they had thought about it and in some cases practice it.
Business surprising that no one did die.
I mean I think knock on wood. I think we're all very lucky that there were no fatalities or serious injuries here and very thankful for that.
What's your reaction to seeing the death of a little officer?
Some of this people have left over here.
My reaction is the amazing power of nature and then how confined it was.
You see this path of destruction that knocked down trees and houses, yet a house or a building, 25 yards to the left or right was unscathed.
Those two things I think were the things that struck me the most.
What does any idea of dollar figures is?

Yeah, but that's one of the things that I'm talking to the installation commander here about and we need to put to make a good assessment here and put a bill on it and then get on with putting things back in place.
Did you have equipment overturned? I understood there might have been some helicopter to make them.
I haven't heard anything about damage to any aviation systems but there were vehicles overturned and damaged.
Do you undergo these now? I don't know particularly who what contractor will do that and that's one of the things that we have to put together a list of what's damaged but needs to be fixed.
And that's part of an assessment that's going on right now.
How's the military taking care of this place and are they paying them for places to live?
Yeah, every one of the families I talked to today said they were have been very well cared for.
We got them into temporary lodging and some of them have already moved into new homes.
And so they're in the process of, I saw one family that was in the process of going through the old house with some friends loading it on a truck and moving it over to a new place.
So far the reaction has been very, very quick and very good.
I think for us and one of the things I'm very concerned about is the claims process.
And all claims processes can be tedious.
What I've told my lawyers is to get as many people out here as we need to so that we can help the soldiers and the families get the claims filed.
I'd like to see all the claims filed in about 45 days.
We don't want you to drag this out.
We need to get it here.
And we're going to put enough people out here to make sure that that happens in a timely fashion.

I've heard my ignorance on the issue of how the Army works but why are you being here and you said you're going to put a dollar amount and you just report back to your higher ups and then it just comes from Army money, the government money.
Well, we'll figure out what needs to be done here.
We'll cost it out and then we'll work with Congress to get the money that we need to get this back, the installation back to where it needs to be.
You worry about getting that money or all the money you need?
No, I don't think we should.
I don't think you can worry about that right now.
No problem with the new Congress.
I can't imagine.
I can't imagine that.
No problem with new homes.
There are some concerns and questions about who we take responsibility for that.
Whether it's a privatized housing.
Yeah, we have to work our way through that.
I don't think we all know fully and appreciate the impact that the privatization will have on this.
So we have to sort our way through that.
How does the reaction here in Portland would represent the whole Army family that together needs to be done?
Well, I mean, that's kind of what I said, that the two things that stuck out most were resilience and teamwork.
And that release, or those two things really represent what the Army family is all about.
And just to watch everybody here, again, not just the folks on the installation, but the community
wrapping their arms around these soldiers and families and helping them get them back on their feet.
And it's just a team effort.
Sir, do you know if any of the storm victims are actually deployed overseas and not able to deal with this?
I did not hear of anyone in that category.
A lot of people were away from Fort Leonard Wood on vacation.
Some in the local area here, relatively close in Missouri.
But I didn't hear of anyone who was deployed.
General, are the troops all back now from Christmas' accident?
They're coming back.
I think they had almost all of the 6,000 folks back by yesterday, but I think there's a few more days to get everybody back here.
Are there shelters on post where people can go?
Is there a unit?
Of all the families I talked to, they did not go to a shelter.
Are there any shelters?
I don't know that.
There are many fixed facilities.
They have shelters.
And they are designated as shelter.
However, the time, the time for the tornado, there was a time for the people to go.
Most of these people said they...
Yes, we have sirens.
Did they go off?
Yeah.
The families I talked to either got the notification off of a radio announcement or they heard the sirens or they heard the big voice.
15 minutes was what I heard.
The sirens?
No, the people once they heard the sirens...
I was noticed the sirens.
They had about 15 minutes, but it really depends on your window.
How close you were in the proximity.
Many of the later, maybe at worst, maybe five or five...
I think the big lesson for everybody is pay attention to the sirens because as we talked to some of the families, they said,
I've heard this before, but we didn't know, but it's when they heard the rumblings.
And they heard the quote, the freight train-like sounds.
That's when they all reacted.
Anyway, I'd just like to, again, thank the local community for the great outpouring of support here.
And as a great team here at Fort Leonard Wood, and we're going to get this place put back together as quickly as we can.
Thank you all very much.
